title: Ephemeral capacity burst & safe GPU replacement - runbook draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a working-runbook for handling short-lived (ephemeral) capacity bursts and performing safe GPU replacements with minimal customer impact. It focuses on: emergency capacity injection, node cordon/drain patterns that avoid mass evictions, preserving KV/prefix caches, and safe rollback steps if replacement degrades latency or cost.

Scope and assumptions:
- Applies to hosted and dedicated clusters running the rwinf serving runtime.
- Cluster is Kubernetes-based with a mix of preemptible and reserved GPU nodes.
- We assume access to: kubectl, rwinfctl (internal CLI), cluster autoscaler dashboards, and access to the SRE oncall rotation.
- This is a draft: test all commands in staging before prod use.

Alert triggers (high-level):
1) Latency spike: p95 token latency > 600ms for 5+ minutes OR request queue length > 500 for an entire AZ.
2) Capacity pressure: pending pods scheduling > 200 for > 3 minutes and autoscaler not adding nodes.
3) Hardware failure syndromes: repeated ECC errors, GPU driver faults, unavailable NVLINK fabric, or node flakiness in node-exporter metrics.
4) Thermal/BIOS alerts: GPU temp > 85C sustained or fan failure alerts from hw-monitor.

Initial triage (first 10 minutes):
- Pager escalation: page SRE oncall (Primary) and post to #sre-oncall and #infra-urgent with short summary and screenshots of metrics.
- Snapshot telemetry: pull p95/p99 token latency, qps, scheduling queue, node gpu_utilization, node temperature, error logs (dmesg, nvidia-smi).
- Check autoscaler: is cluster-autoscaler reporting failures? Look at events: kubectl -n kube-system logs deployment/cluster-autoscaler --tail=200.
- Quick mitigation: enable traffic throttles in edge-router if inference latency is degraded (lowers tail risk while we stabilize).

Emergency capacity injection (fast path):
1) If autoscaler stuck, manually spin up ephemeral nodes: rwinfctl infra spawn --pool ephemeral-gpu --count 4 --flavor g5dn. Confirm node readiness with kubectl get nodes -l ephemeral=true.
2) Patch serving deployment to accept burst capacity: kubectl patch deployment redwood-serving --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/template/spec/containers/0/env/0/value","value":"burst=on"}]'
3) Monitor queue drain and latency. If pods schedule and queue drops, leave nodes until traffic stabilizes.
4) Document costs and create RED-INC ticket to capture the incident and spend.

Safe cordon & drain pattern (minimize evictions):
Goal: remove a node for GPU replacement while keeping in-flight requests and cached KV prefixes safe.
Pre-steps (10-15m):
- Identify target node: kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep <node-name>. Confirm GPU health: ssh node; nvidia-smi -q | grep -E "(ECC|Xid|Temperature)".
- Annotate node to prevent new prefix cache priming: kubectl annotate node <node> redwood/maintenance=true --overwrite.
- Scale down low-priority workloads: kubectl scale deployment low-priority-workload --replicas=0 -n workloads.
- Migrate KV cache (best-effort): rwinfctl cache migrate --from-node <node> --to-selector "pool=ephemeral" --grace 120. This attempts to warm caches on destination nodes prior to draining.

Cordoning and staged drain (recommended):
1) Cordon node: kubectl cordon <node>  # prevents new pods from scheduling
2) Evict non-serving, non-stateful pods first: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='app!=redwood-serving' --grace-period=60 --timeout=300s
3) Wait for running serving pods to finish active requests (monitor envoy/ingress metrics and runtime connections). If serving pods have long-lived streams, use graceful drain with connection-aware drain: rwinfctl node-drain --node <node> --grace 300 --conn-check 30
4) After app pods are mostly drained, scale up temporary serving pods on replacement nodes by increasing deployment replicas: kubectl scale deployment redwood-serving --replicas=<current+N> --namespace=redwood

Replacement and verification:
- Power cycle or pull GPU per hardware SOP. On replacement node, run post-replacement checks:
  - nvidia-smi --query-gpu=name,driver_version,serial,temperature.gpu,utilization.gpu --format=csv -l 1
  - run gpu-diagnostics.sh --quick (internal tool)
- Re-enable node: kubectl uncordon <node> once kubelet reports Ready and diagnostics pass.
- Validate that serving pods scheduled onto node and pass healthchecks: kubectl get pods -o wide -n redwood | grep <node>.
- Watch metrics for 15 minutes: p50/p95 latency, error rates, queue length. If any regression >10% sustained, mark node unschedulable and rollback.

Rollback steps (if replacement causes regression):
- Immediately cordon the node: kubectl cordon <node>.
- If new pods are unhealthy on that node, evict serving pods and re-schedule: kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=30 --force.
- Reintroduce previous node (if available) or spin up reserve nodes: rwinfctl infra spawn --pool reserved-gpu --count 2.
- Repoint traffic gradually off the problematic node by adjusting rollout weights in the console or Route 53 traffic-split config.
- Create and assign incident owner to follow up with hardware/vendor (RED-INC-1987).

Post-incident playbook for capacity-adds (planned expansion):
- Pre-warm caches: deploy canary traffic to new nodes using rwinfctl canary --targets "pool=new-capacity" --qps 10 --duration 10m.
- Gradual scale: add nodes in small batches (2–4) and observe per-batch for 20m before next batch.
- Autoscaler tuning: verify cluster-autoscaler limits and add fallback policies for max-surge.

Run validation checklist (post-work):
- p50/p95/p99 token latency baseline restored.
- No 5xx error spike in requests.
- Node-level: GPU driver version consistent across pool, driver has no error logs.
- Cache hit rates restored to normal.
- Billing spike documented and reviewed by infra finance.

Escalation matrix and contacts:
- SRE oncall (Primary): see PagerDuty rotation; fallback to SRE lead Omar Haddad.
- Serving runtime eng: channel @serving-runtime (Linnea Berg), oncall rotation for runtime.
- Hardware vendor contacts: vendor-support@partners.example with RED-INC id.

Notes & open questions (draft):
- Need a standardized rwinfctl subcommand for cache pre-warm that integrates with autoscaler decisions.
- How to better shard priority to avoid low-priority eviction of mid-latency critical tasks? Proposal in linked Confluence.
- Consider a small reserved buffer of non-preemptible nodes per AZ to avoid cross-AZ flapping.

Postmortem template (for incident owners):
- Summary: 1–2 sentences.
- Timeline: minute-level events from detection to resolution.
- Root cause: hardware/software/config contributing factors.
- Mitigations: immediate and long-term.
- Action items: owner, ETA, ticket link.

Appendix: useful commands
- kubectl cordon <node>
- kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60 --timeout=300s
- kubectl uncordon <node>
- kubectl get events --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp | tail -n 200
- rwinfctl infra spawn --pool ephemeral-gpu --count 4 --flavor g5dn
- rwinfctl cache migrate --from-node <node> --to-selector "pool=ephemeral" --grace 120
- rwinfctl node-drain --node <node> --grace 300 --conn-check 30  

Revision history:
- 2025-11-18: initial notes (Priya)
- 2026-01-09: added cache migration steps (Omar)
- 2026-02-22: expanded rollback criteria and commands (Linnea)

This is a living document. Add test results and keep commands updated when rwinfctl/kubectl flags change.
